overview.title: What Is a CDN?
overview.p1: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a network of edge servers distributed across multiple regions. When a user visits your site, the CDN routes the request to the node physically closest to them instead of forcing every request back to a single origin server, shortening the data path, reducing latency, and easing the load on your origin infrastructure.
overview.p2: Kineticlinks operates over 100 edge nodes across Asia-Pacific, North America, and Europe, using intelligent routing to continuously measure latency and congestion at each node and automatically select the fastest path. Whether your users are in Taiwan, mainland China, Southeast Asia, or Western markets, they get access speeds close to a local server.
overview.p3: Beyond acceleration, a CDN is also your first line of defense against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. Kineticlinks provides terabit-scale scrubbing capacity that filters malicious traffic at the edge before it ever reaches your origin server, keeping your business running without interruption.

article_domain_hijacking.title: Your Transfer Lock Won't Stop a Hijack: What Domain Security Settings Actually Cover
article_domain_hijacking.excerpt: Most people enable transfer lock and feel protected. But that lock lives inside your registrar account — and an attacker who takes the account simply switches it off.
article_domain_hijacking.lead: In almost every domain hijacking case, the victim had transfer lock enabled. The problem is where that lock sits: **it's a setting inside your registrar account, and the account is what's being attacked**. Once someone is in, turning the lock off is one click. This covers what four common protections actually cover, and why some widely-recommended measures don't defend against account-level compromise at all.

seo.title: Domain Hijacking Defence | Why Transfer Lock Isn't Enough
seo.description: Transfer lock lives inside the registrar account and falls with it. What transfer lock, 2FA, DNSSEC and registry lock each cover, the early warning signs of a hijack, and how fast you must act.
seo.keywords: domain hijacking, transfer lock, registry lock, DNSSEC, domain security, stolen domain, clientTransferProhibited, two-factor authentication

s1.title: There Are Two Locks, and Most People Only Have the Outer One
s1.p1: Domain transfer locking exists at two levels with confusingly similar names and very different strength. The toggle in a normal registrar dashboard is **clientTransferProhibited**, set and removed by the registrar. The other is a **registry lock**, enforced by the registry that runs the top-level domain.
s1.p2: The difference is who can remove it. The first can be removed from inside your account; the second cannot. An attacker holding your registrar credentials can switch off clientTransferProhibited themselves, whereas lifting a registry lock requires registrar staff to request it from the registry and pass out-of-band verification — in practice often a phone call with a passphrase.
s1.p3: The table lays out four common measures. The third column is the point — what each one **fails to stop** is where the breach actually happens.

table.caption: What four domain protections cover. Only registry lock survives a compromised account.
table.r1c3: Removal by whoever holds the account
table.r2c2: Direct login from a leaked password
table.r3c2: Tampering with DNS responses in transit
table.r4c2: Changes even when the account is breached

s2.title: Three Early Signs People Miss
s2.intro: A hijack is rarely instantaneous — there's usually an interval where it can be stopped. Three signals worth verifying immediately:
s2.r1_title: Password reset emails you didn't request
s2.r1_desc: A reset notification from your registrar that you didn't trigger means someone is attempting to take the account. The email alone doesn't mean they've succeeded, but it's the earliest signal. Check at the same time whether the account's contact address has been changed — attackers often swap the email first, after which no further notifications reach you.
s2.r2_desc: WHOIS contact data or nameserver settings changing without your action is clear evidence of compromise. Nameserver changes are especially dangerous, since they redirect traffic while the domain remains registered to you — which is why people often assume "the domain is still mine, so it must be fine".
s2.r3_title: Auth codes or transfer notices you didn't initiate
s2.r3_desc: A notification that an EPP auth code was issued, or a transfer confirmation you didn't request, means a transfer is already in motion. Timing is critical here — if the losing registrar takes no action, the transfer auto-approves after five days, and those five days are your window to stop it.

s3.title: Why Registrar-Level Protection Isn't Enough
s3.p1: Those three signs share a property: **they all occur after the attacker is already inside the account**. And once the account is lost, every setting within it is changeable — transfer lock, contact address, nameservers, all of it. That's why "I have the lock enabled" isn't a security guarantee.
s3.p2: Two-factor authentication genuinely raises the bar and belongs on every domain. But it defends against leaked passwords, not social engineering — an attacker impersonating the registrant to support staff bypasses people, not systems. In hijacks of corporate domains, that path is far from rare.
s3.callout: If it does happen, speed decides the outcome. Practical experience puts most successful recoveries within 24 to 48 hours, with odds falling the longer it takes. So on discovering something wrong, the order is: contact your registrar's abuse or security team immediately and ask them to lock the domain, while preserving evidence (WHOIS history, screenshots, timeline, proof of ownership) — rather than trying to change settings back yourself first. If it has already been transferred out, contact the gaining registrar too, and consider ICANN's Transfer Dispute Resolution Policy.
s3.p3: As for registry lock, it's the only measure that survives account compromise — at the cost of flexibility. Unlocking is a manual process taking hours to a business day, which suits domains that rarely change but absolutely cannot fail. **Note that this service is typically offered by enterprise or corporate registrars; most consumer registrars don't provide it**, so confirm availability before relying on it.

s4.title: What DNSSEC Is Commonly Mistaken For
s4.p1: DNSSEC appears on nearly every domain security checklist, but the problem it solves isn't hijacking. Its purpose is to let resolvers verify that a DNS response genuinely came from the domain's authoritative servers and wasn't altered in transit — it defends against cache poisoning and man-in-the-middle tampering.
s4.p2: But if an attacker logs into your registrar account and openly changes the NS records, those new records get signed correctly too. **DNSSEC raises no alarm, because from the protocol's perspective that was a legitimate change made by the domain owner**. So enable DNSSEC, but don't count it as part of your anti-hijacking defence — they address different threats.

s5.title: Three Layers of Defence
s5.intro: By cost and effectiveness, build in this order:
s5.l1_title: 1. Treat the registrar account as critical
s5.l1_desc: This is the most basic and most effective layer, because it's the actual attack surface. Enable two-factor authentication, use a unique password, and **make sure the account's contact address isn't hosted on the domain itself** — otherwise a problem with the domain leaves you unable to receive the verification email, a deadlock.
s5.l2_title: 2. Enable every available lock, and re-check regularly
s5.l2_desc: Transfer lock doesn't stop account compromise, but it does stop unauthorised transfer requests, and it costs nothing. The key is **re-checking** — locks get "temporarily" removed during a migration and never restored. Put it on a quarterly checklist.
s5.l3_title: 3. Evaluate registry lock for critical domains
s5.l3_desc: If losing a domain would halt operations, registry lock is worth evaluating. It makes routine changes cumbersome, which is precisely the point. If this matters to you, confirm your registrar offers it before committing.

s6.title: Three Things to Check Right Now
s6.intro: No tooling required — a registrar login is enough:
s6.c1_desc: Visible in the Domain Status field of a WHOIS lookup. Its absence means transfer lock is off, and anyone obtaining an auth code can initiate a transfer.
s6.c2_title: Whether the account email is independent of this domain
s6.c2_desc: If the registrar account uses `admin@your-domain`, and that domain is what you're protecting, you have a circular dependency. Moving to an independent address costs nothing and matters enormously.
s6.c3_desc: Check **both** the registrar account and the email account it's tied to. Protecting the registrar while leaving the mailbox on a password alone leaves a password-reset bypass wide open.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: The real weak point in domain security isn't the domain — it's **the account that manages it**. Transfer lock and DNSSEC each have value, but neither defends against account takeover, and account takeover is the actual route in the overwhelming majority of hijacks.
s7.p2: So the priority is: protect the registrar account as you would any critical credential (2FA, independent email, unique password), then consider the rest. If you're evaluating registrars, support for these options is worth comparing — our domain registration guide covers the other criteria worth weighing.

article_quality_monitoring.title: One Test Proves Nothing: Why Cross-Border Quality Needs Continuous Monitoring
article_quality_monitoring.excerpt: Cross-border problems are overwhelmingly time-of-day. You test when users complain and everything looks fine — they aren't mistaken, you're measuring at the wrong hour.
article_quality_monitoring.lead: "Users say it's unusable in the evening, but every test I run looks fine." This is the most common dispute in cross-border services, and usually neither side is wrong — **cross-border quality varies substantially by hour**, and a daytime measurement says nothing about the evening. A single test answers "how is this second", when the question you need answered is "what are users actually getting". Only continuous monitoring closes that gap.

seo.title: Monitoring Cross-Border Connectivity | Why One Test Isn't Enough
seo.description: Cross-border issues are mostly time-of-day, so single tests misrepresent reality. What four testing approaches each reveal, three problems only continuous monitoring catches, and which metrics to track.
seo.keywords: connectivity monitoring, cross-border network monitoring, three-network monitoring, speed test API, peak hour congestion, packet loss monitoring

s1.title: The Second You Measured vs the Hour Users Lived Through
s1.p1: The key difference from local networking: local faults tend to be persistent — broken stays broken — while cross-border problems are **almost always time-of-day**. International gateways congest at peak, routes shift at particular hours, carrier interconnects load up at night. All of these make one link behave completely differently depending on when you look.
s1.p2: So when a user reports stuttering at 8pm and you test at 10am the next morning, "everything looks fine" is the expected result. It doesn't mean the problem isn't real; it means you weren't measuring while it was happening.
s1.p3: The table compares four common approaches. The third column is the point — what each one cannot see.

table.caption: What four testing approaches cover. Only the last reflects what users actually encounter.
table.r1c3: Actual data from when it broke
table.r2c2: Quality of your line to theirs
table.r2c3: Quality of the user's own line
table.r3c3: How each varies across the day

s2.title: Three Problems Only Continuous Monitoring Catches
s2.intro: A single test is statistically unlikely to land on any of these:
s2.r1_desc: International gateway capacity is shared, and as evening usage climbs, latency and loss degrade together. That degradation usually concentrates into a few hours — while most testing happens during office hours, missing it entirely. Proving it exists requires continuous data spanning those hours.
s2.r2_desc: Cross-border routes aren't fixed; carriers adjust them for cost and load. A single change can move latency from 80ms to 200ms with no notification at all. Without a long-run baseline you won't even know it got worse — because you don't remember what it used to be.
s2.r3_desc: The three carriers run separate international gateways, so degradation doesn't arrive in step. Mobile might be badly affected in one window while Telecom and Unicom are fine. Even a test covering all three is still one slice of time — it can't reveal which carrier has a recurring problem in which hours.

s3.title: What to Monitor
s3.p1: The metric priority is the same as for single readings: **loss first, latency second, bandwidth last**. But continuous monitoring adds a more important dimension — **variation**. A link steady at 120ms is usually more usable than one swinging between 60ms and 250ms, even though the latter has the better average.
s3.p2: So look at distribution, not just absolute values. For any metric, what matters is behaviour during peak hours rather than the mean — an average dilutes the three bad hours until the report looks healthy, while those diluted hours are exactly what users experienced.
s3.callout: Match check frequency to the problem you're hunting. Hourly is enough to catch an evening peak; brief routing instability needs more. But higher isn't automatically better — frequent checks are themselves traffic, and they generate large volumes of uninformative data points. Decide what question you're answering, then set the frequency.
s3.p3: One thing easily overlooked: **checks must originate from the user's network**. Testing from your own facility measures your line. If your users are on China Mobile, the test has to run on Mobile's network, or the data has nothing to do with their experience. This is why cross-border monitoring generally requires probes inside the target market.

s4.title: Same Logic as Certificate Monitoring
s4.p1: If you read our piece on certificate expiry monitoring, the argument is structurally identical: **a one-off check cannot prove a continuous state**. There it was "renewal succeeded doesn't mean the certificate is being served"; here it's "fine this second doesn't mean users are fine".
s4.p2: The remedy is the same too — replace one-off checks with scheduled continuous ones, run from outside and from where users actually are. The only difference is that certificate monitoring cares about correctness of state, while network monitoring cares about the distribution of quality.

s5.title: Three Layers of Implementation
s5.intro: From the basics up, build this in stages:
s5.l1_desc: Start recording normal latency and loss before anything is wrong. Without a baseline, no later number can be judged good or bad. The value of this step only becomes visible after the fact — by which point it's too late to create retroactively.
s5.l2_title: 2. Cover all three carriers and the full day
s5.l2_desc: Checks need to cover Telecom, Unicom and Mobile separately, across a complete day-night cycle. Testing only during office hours systematically misses the hours you most need to see.
s5.l3_title: 3. Feed it into your existing monitoring
s5.l3_desc: Connectivity data living on its own separate dashboard is data nobody checks regularly. Better to pull it via API into whatever monitoring or alerting the team already uses, alongside other metrics — that's what gets anomalies noticed rather than reported to you by users.

s6.title: Three Things to Settle Before Monitoring
s6.intro: Work these out before configuring anything:
s6.c1_title: Decide which target nodes to monitor
s6.c1_desc: Origin, CDN nodes, or both? Monitoring only the CDN hides origin problems when fetches slow down; monitoring only the origin doesn't reflect the path users take.
s6.c2_title: Confirm probes sit on the user's side
s6.c2_desc: Cross-border monitoring requires checks originating in the target market, split across the three carriers. Testing inward from outside measures the reverse direction, and the two aren't necessarily symmetric.
s6.c3_title: Decide how the data gets used
s6.c3_desc: Reviewing trends by hand, or threshold-based automatic alerting? The latter needs an API to feed existing systems. This determines whether you need a web tool or a programmable interface.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: Users reporting "slow in the evening" and your tests looking clean can both be true. Cross-border quality is a distribution that moves over time, not a fixed number, and one test samples a single point of it — usually the least important point, during office hours.
s7.p2: To check current three-carrier connectivity, the free tier of our speed test platform covers it. If you need scheduled checks, long-run trends, or the data fed into your own monitoring and alerting, the commercial API provides programmable access.

article_reading_speedtest.title: Reading Speed Test Results: Why Enough Bandwidth Still Feels Slow Cross-Border
article_reading_speedtest.excerpt: Most people read a speed test as one number — download Mbps. That's the least useful figure for cross-border services. Latency and packet loss decide what users feel, and their effects multiply rather than add.
article_reading_speedtest.lead: "We're paying for 1Gbps — why do users still say it's slow?" That question almost always rests on one assumption: that bandwidth is a synonym for connection quality. In cross-border scenarios **bandwidth usually isn't the bottleneck** — latency and packet loss are, and their damage to real throughput compounds. This explains what each number on a speed test actually means, and which one to read first.

seo.title: Reading Speed Test Results | Latency, Jitter & Packet Loss
seo.description: A speed test isn't just download speed. What bandwidth, latency, jitter, and packet loss each mean, why loss hurts cross-border transfer far more than limited bandwidth, and why China's three carriers must be measured separately.
seo.keywords: speed test, latency, jitter, packet loss, RTT, three-network test, cross-border connectivity, network quality

s1.title: The Five Numbers on a Speed Test
s1.p1: A complete test reports bandwidth, latency, jitter, packet loss and — for China connectivity — separate figures for each of the three carriers. Most people read only the first, which is often the number least connected to what users experience.
s1.p2: Bandwidth measures how many cars the road can hold. Latency and packet loss measure whether the cars actually move. An eight-lane road that jams constantly can mean a longer commute than a clear four-lane one, and cross-border links are almost always the former.
s1.p3: The table lists all five with reference thresholds. Those in the third column come from established standards for real-time communications and serve as a starting point.

table.caption: Five speed test metrics and common reference thresholds. Packet loss deserves the most attention cross-border.
table.r4c2: Share of packets lost in transit
table.r5c3: One carrier alone doesn't show the picture

s2.title: Why Packet Loss Matters Far More Than Bandwidth
s2.intro: This isn't a rule of thumb — it's a mathematical property of TCP. Three reasons:
s2.r1_desc: TCP reads a lost packet as "the network is congested" and reduces its sending rate. That's sensible on a local network, but on cross-border links loss often comes from line quality rather than congestion — so TCP misreads it and throttles itself, and the bandwidth you paid for goes unused.
s2.r2_title: Throughput is inversely proportional to the square root of loss
s2.r2_desc: This is the relationship the Mathis equation describes: throughput is roughly segment size divided by round-trip time, multiplied by one over the square root of the loss rate. In practice, loss worsening from 0.1% to 1% cuts throughput to about a third — entirely independent of your bandwidth.
s2.r3_title: Latency amplifies the damage from loss
s2.r3_desc: In the same formula, throughput is also inversely proportional to RTT. So on cross-border links high latency and loss compound: 1% loss on a local network may be a mild slowdown, but the same 1% over a 200ms path drives real throughput down to unusable levels.

s3.title: What This Looks Like in Practice
s3.p1: The classic symptom is "the speed test looks fine but users keep complaining". Most tools display peak bandwidth by default, and a peak is measured in the most favourable instant — it cannot reveal time-of-day packet loss.
s3.p2: Page loading is another common case. A page pulls dozens of resources, each needing connection setup and transfer. With high latency those round trips accumulate, and retransmissions from loss add more, so what users perceive is "the page is stuck" rather than "the download is slow". This is precisely why a bandwidth figure alone misleads.
s3.callout: A practical reading order: packet loss first, then latency, and bandwidth last. If loss exceeds 1%, the other numbers barely matter — fix the loss, because adding bandwidth is simply wasted money until you do. That order is the reverse of most people's instinct, but it matches how TCP actually behaves.
s3.p3: Worth adding: these thresholds are general starting points, not hard standards. Real-time voice and video are especially sensitive to jitter (noticeable beyond 30ms), while bulk transfer cares more about the combination of loss and latency. Read them against what your service actually does.

s4.title: Why China Connectivity Needs Three Separate Tests
s4.p1: China Telecom, Unicom and Mobile each run their own backbone and international gateways, and interconnection between them is uneven. The same overseas node might sit 80ms away for a Telecom user and 200ms with packet loss for a Mobile user — **that isn't measurement error, the traffic genuinely takes different paths**.
s4.p2: So one carrier's result can't stand in for the whole. If your users span all three but you test through one, two thirds of your user experience is unmeasured. That's why cross-border testing tools present the carriers separately: not for presentation, but because a single figure is meaningless here.

s5.title: Three Levels of Interpretation
s5.intro: Given a set of results, work through them in this order:
s5.l1_desc: This is the priority metric. Below 0.1% is normal; above 1% materially damages TCP throughput; above 3% users are probably already complaining. Loss usually originates along the path rather than at either end, so adding bandwidth or better hardware on your side won't improve it.
s5.l2_desc: Latency is set by physical distance and routing, so improvement means taking a different path — serving from a nearby CDN node rather than sending users all the way to origin. Jitter reflects path stability; high jitter usually means congestion or unstable routing in between.
s5.l3_desc: Only once the first two are within reasonable ranges does bandwidth become the real constraint, and only then is buying more of it worthwhile. Reversed — adding bandwidth while loss is unresolved — the spend never shows up in what users feel.

s6.title: Three Things to Get Right Before Testing
s6.intro: Results are only interpretable if the test itself is sound:
s6.c1_title: Test from where users actually are
s6.c1_desc: Testing from your own facility or office measures your line, not theirs. That's doubly true cross-border: the test has to originate in the target market.
s6.c2_desc: With a CDN in front, you may be measuring the nearest edge node rather than the origin. The two produce very different numbers, so establish which layer you're testing before reading anything into it.
s6.c3_desc: Cross-border problems are overwhelmingly time-of-day. A single test proves things were fine for one second and says nothing about any other hour. That deserves its own treatment, which we cover separately in a piece on continuous monitoring.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: The download figure printed largest on a speed test is usually the least informative one cross-border. What users feel is decided by loss and latency, and the two multiply — a mathematical property of TCP, not a tuning problem.
s7.p2: If you need to see outbound quality separately across China's three carriers, our free online speed test shows latency and loss for Telecom, Unicom and Mobile individually.

article_acme_challenges.title: Where Certificate Automation Actually Breaks: Choosing an ACME Challenge Type
article_acme_challenges.excerpt: People assume installing Certbot means automation is done. What actually blocks them is picking the wrong challenge type — HTTP-01 fails behind a CDN, and wildcard certificates can't use it at all.
article_acme_challenges.lead: "Just install Certbot" is the most common misconception about certificate automation. The tooling isn't the hard part. What actually blocks people is **choosing the wrong challenge type** — and the problem usually doesn't surface at install time. It surfaces when you put the service behind a CDN, or the first time you request a wildcard certificate. Each of the three challenge types has hard constraints worth knowing before you commit.

s1.title: The Blocker Is the Challenge Type, Not the Tool
s1.p1: The ACME protocol requires you to prove you control a domain before it issues a certificate. That proof is the challenge, and there are three main types, each asking you to place specified content somewhere different: a path on your website, a DNS TXT record, or the TLS handshake itself.
s1.p2: Most tutorials hand you a single Certbot command, which defaults to HTTP-01. On a single machine facing the internet directly, that works. But add any architectural complexity — a CDN in front, several backends, or a need for wildcards — and HTTP-01 starts failing, usually without an error that says "you should be using a different challenge type".
s1.p3: The table below sets out how each works and what constrains it. The third column is what should drive the decision.

table.caption: How the three ACME challenge types work and their hard constraints. The fourth row is a newer type not yet in production.
table.r1c2: Serve a file at a specific path for the CA to fetch
table.r1c3: Needs port 80 open; fails behind CDNs and multi-node setups; no wildcards
table.r2c2: Publish a specified TXT record under the domain
table.r2c3: Only option for wildcards; needs DNS API access and propagation waits
table.r3c2: Serve a special certificate during the TLS handshake
table.r3c3: Needs direct control of port 443; unusable behind a CDN; no wildcards
table.r4c2: One standing authorisation record, no repeated updates
table.r4c3: IETF draft; check Let's Encrypt for current production availability

s2.title: Three Situations Where HTTP-01 Fails
s2.intro: HTTP-01 requires the CA to read a specific file from your server over the public internet. These three architectures break that assumption:
s2.r1_title: The service sits behind a CDN
s2.r1_desc: The CA's request hits a CDN node first, while the validation file lives on the origin. Unless the CDN is configured to pass `/.well-known/acme-challenge/` through to the origin, the CA gets a cached response or a 404. This is the most common case for teams in Taiwan and Hong Kong, since cross-border services almost always front with a CDN.
s2.r2_desc: The load balancer routes the CA's request to one machine at random, but the validation file only exists on whichever machine initiated the request. That's a 1-in-N hit rate, and each retry may land somewhere different. This failure is particularly irritating because it's intermittent — sometimes it passes, sometimes it doesn't.
s2.r3_desc: Where security policy closes port 80, or the service is only offered internally, HTTP-01 simply cannot work. That includes API domains you only want reachable from specific sources.

s3.title: What DNS-01 Costs You
s3.p1: DNS-01 solves all of the above — it never needs the CA to reach your server, only to resolve a DNS record. So it doesn't matter whether you're behind a CDN, how many machines you run, or whether port 80 is open. That's why multi-node architectures almost always end up on DNS-01.
s3.p2: It carries its own cost, though. Every issuance requires adding a TXT record, meaning your automation must hold **DNS provider API credentials**. Those credentials have to reach every machine or CI environment that performs renewals — and DNS access is high-risk, since holding it means being able to repoint your domain.
s3.callout: The other practical pain is propagation delay. A TXT record isn't instantly visible on every DNS server, so automation has to wait, and there's no standard answer for how long. Too short and validation fails; too long and every issuance drags. As lifetimes shorten and renewals multiply, that accumulated waiting becomes significant.
s3.p3: Worth noting: in February 2026 Let's Encrypt proposed **DNS-PERSIST-01**, which replaces the repeated updates with a single standing authorisation record bound to a specific ACME account — aimed squarely at both pain points above. It remains an IETF draft; the announced production target was Q2 2026, so check Let's Encrypt's own announcements for current availability. Note too that once authorisation is persistent, protecting the ACME account key matters correspondingly more.

s4.title: The Hard Constraint on Wildcards
s4.p1: If you need a wildcard like `*.example.com`, the decision is already made: **only DNS-01 can issue one**. Neither HTTP-01 nor TLS-ALPN-01 can produce wildcard certificates. This isn't a configuration issue; it's a protocol-level constraint.
s4.p2: It's worth knowing early, because it works backwards into your choice of DNS provider. If your registrar or DNS service offers no API, you can't automate DNS-01, which means no automatically-renewed wildcard — you'd be adding TXT records by hand every time. With lifetimes already at 200 days and heading to 47, manual handling isn't a viable long-term plan.

s5.title: Three Implementation Decisions
s5.intro: In practice the choice reduces to three questions:
s5.l1_title: 1. Is there a CDN or load balancer in front?
s5.l1_desc: If so, rule out HTTP-01 and TLS-ALPN-01 and use DNS-01. You can force HTTP-01 to work by configuring the CDN to pass the validation path through to origin, but that's an extra special-case rule to maintain, and it's easily broken by unrelated CDN changes.
s5.l2_desc: If yes, DNS-01 is the only option. If your subdomains are few and stable, a SAN certificate listing them all avoids wildcards — but every new subdomain then requires reissuing, so weigh that against how often they change.
s5.l3_title: 3. Does your DNS provider expose an API?
s5.l3_desc: This is the prerequisite for DNS-01. When choosing a registrar or DNS service, treat API support as a requirement rather than a bonus. Plan credential storage too — putting DNS API keys directly in config files on every server turns your certificate automation into a security weakness.

s6.title: Three Things to Establish First
s6.c1_title: List every domain and subdomain needing a certificate
s6.c1_desc: This determines whether you need wildcards, which determines the challenge type. Discovering the wildcard requirement afterwards means rebuilding the whole flow.
s6.c2_title: Check your DNS provider's API and permission granularity
s6.c2_desc: Beyond whether an API exists, check whether it can issue scoped tokens limited to TXT records on specific domains. Full-access keys distributed across machines carry too much risk.
s6.c3_title: Recognise that validation and deployment are separate
s6.c3_desc: Obtaining the certificate is step one. It still has to reach every TLS-terminating endpoint and take effect, which ACME tooling generally doesn't handle. Decide who owns that half before you start.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: The hard part of certificate automation was never installing Certbot; it's picking the right challenge for your actual architecture. The logic is short: **a CDN in front or a wildcard requirement means DNS-01** — and committing to DNS-01 means first confirming your DNS provider has an API, then managing that key carefully.
s7.p2: If you'd rather not handle DNS API key distribution and multi-node deployment yourself, our SSL automation platform combines validation and delivery in one flow: the platform performs DNS validation and pushes issued certificates straight to CDN nodes.

article_cert_monitoring.title: Certificate Monitoring: A Successful Renewal Doesn't Mean Users Got the New Certificate
article_cert_monitoring.excerpt: Most teams monitor whether renewal ran successfully. What actually causes incidents is renewal succeeding while the certificate never reaches every endpoint — and only one kind of check catches that.
article_cert_monitoring.lead: Once ACME automation is in place, most people stop thinking about certificates. Certificate incidents don't disappear though — they change shape: the renewal log says success, the CA portal shows issued, and users still get a browser warning. The reason is that **a successful renewal and a certificate actually being served are two independent things**, and most monitoring only watches the first.

seo.title: Certificate Expiry Monitoring | Why Auto-Renewal Still Breaks
seo.description: A successful renewal doesn't mean your site is fine. What four kinds of monitoring catch and miss, three ways renewal succeeds but still breaks, tiered alert thresholds, and the only check that proves users are unaffected.
seo.keywords: certificate expiry monitoring, SSL certificate monitoring, certificate alerts, auto-renewal failure, certificate deployment, TLS monitoring

s1.title: "Renewal Succeeded" and "Everything's Fine" Are Different Claims
s1.p1: A full certificate update has four stages: request from the CA, complete domain validation, deploy the new certificate to every TLS endpoint, and confirm users actually receive it. ACME tooling handles **the first two**; the third depends on your configuration; and almost nothing does the fourth for you automatically.
s1.p2: That's where the gap opens. A renewal log reading `success` means the certificate was obtained, not that it's being served. Deployment and reload still sit in between, and a failure at either never shows up in the renewal log.
s1.p3: The table below lays out four common monitoring approaches. The important column is the third — what each one **misses** is exactly where incidents happen.

table.caption: What four monitoring approaches cover. Only the last proves users are unaffected.
table.r2c3: Whether the new certificate is served
table.r3c1: Local check of the certificate file
table.r3c3: CDN nodes, load balancers, other endpoints
table.r4c3: (the only approach that proves nothing is wrong)

s2.title: Three Ways Renewal Succeeds and Things Still Break
s2.intro: All three are real situations where the renewal log said success and users still saw warnings:
s2.r1_title: The new certificate didn't reach every endpoint
s2.r1_desc: If traffic passes through a CDN, load balancer, or several backends, the certificate has to update everywhere TLS terminates. Updating the origin while CDN nodes still serve the old certificate is the most common version. Because only some nodes are affected, reports come in as "some people say it's broken, others say it's fine" — which makes diagnosis harder.
s2.r2_title: Certificate and private key don't match
s2.r2_desc: The certificate is replaced but the private key isn't updated in step (or vice versa), and the service refuses to load it. This usually errors on reload — but if nobody is watching logs, the error gets swallowed and the service keeps running on the old certificate held in memory until it expires.
s2.r3_title: The file updated but the service never reloaded
s2.r3_desc: This is the most insidious one. The certificate file on disk is new, a local check looks fine, but Nginx, Apache, or the application is still using the old certificate loaded into memory at startup. Everything looks correct from the server; connect from outside and you get a certificate about to expire.

s3.title: What to Monitor, and When to Alert
s3.p1: Those three situations point to one principle: **monitoring has to originate outside your network, against the address users actually reach**. A check from inside the facility or on the same machine cannot prove that every layer on the public path received the new certificate.
s3.p2: What you check shouldn't be limited to the expiry date either. Cover at minimum: expiry time, whether the chain is complete (a missing intermediate fails on some clients), whether the served certificate matches the expected domain, and — if you run multiple nodes — whether every node serves the same certificate.
s3.callout: Don't set a single alert threshold. In practice, alert at 60, 30, 14, 7, and 1 day before expiry. The first says "start paying attention"; the last says "handle this now". A single threshold either fires so early it gets dismissed as noise, or so late there's no time to diagnose a failure — and short-lived certificates already compress that diagnostic window.
s3.p3: Also confirm where alerts land. Mail to an unwatched inbox, or a red dot on a dashboard nobody opens, is equivalent to no alerting at all. Route it into a channel the team actually reads, and name someone responsible.

s4.title: Shorter Lifetimes Move This From Optional to Required
s4.p1: When certificates lasted 398 days, you handled this once a year, and imperfect monitoring carried limited risk. Lifetimes dropped to 200 days in March 2026, fall to 100 days in 2027, and to 47 days in 2029 — roughly eight renewals a year at that point.
s4.p2: Every renewal is another chance to fail. Going from once a year to eight times a year means **the same failure rate produces eight times as many incidents**. That's why monitoring stops being a nice-to-have in the short-lifetime era and becomes automation's necessary counterpart: automation makes the frequency survivable, and monitoring is what confirms those automated updates actually took effect.

s5.title: Three Layers of Implementation
s5.intro: From the basics up, this can be built in stages:
s5.l1_desc: The basic version is a scheduled job that opens a TLS connection to each public domain, reads the certificate actually served, and compares the expiry date. On the command line, `openssl s_client -connect <domain>:443 -servername <domain>` shows exactly what the server returns. Wrap that in a schedule with threshold alerting and you've already prevented most incidents.
s5.l2_desc: List everywhere TLS terminates — origin, each CDN node, load balancers, API domains, mail servers. Checking only the main domain misses the rest. If your CDN has multiple nodes, ideally run checks from several regions, since node certificate updates don't always propagate in step.
s5.l3_title: 3. Fold deployment verification into the automation
s5.l3_desc: The fuller approach makes verification part of the renewal flow itself: after issuing and deploying, automatically confirm from outside that the new certificate is being served, and treat a failed confirmation as a failure of the whole flow. Only then does "renewal succeeded" actually mean "users have the new certificate" rather than "the file downloaded".

s6.title: Three Things to Establish First
s6.intro: Before configuring anything, take stock of these:
s6.c1_desc: Main domain, subdomains, API, mail, and each CDN or load balancer node. Endpoints missing from the list won't be monitored, and they'll show users warnings just the same.
s6.c2_desc: The monitoring host must sit outside your network, taking the path users take. Internal checks skip the CDN and external load balancers — precisely the layer most often missed.
s6.c3_desc: Name the channel and the owner. Once thresholds are set, fire a test alert and confirm delivery — plenty of monitoring setups discover on incident day that the notification path broke long ago.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: Certificate automation solves "renewing is tedious". Monitoring solves "did the renewal actually take effect". Both need to exist — automation without monitoring hands a high-frequency process entirely to a mechanism nobody checks, and shrinking lifetimes are pushing that frequency toward eight times a year.
s7.p2: There's a single question that tells you whether your monitoring is sufficient: **does it check the certificate file, or what users actually receive?** If it's the former, it catches none of the three situations described above.

article_domain_transfer.title: Transferring a Domain Won't Take Your Site Down: Process, Auth Codes, and Timing
article_domain_transfer.excerpt: Plenty of people stay with a bad registrar because they fear a transfer will break their site. It won't — a transfer changes who manages the registration, not where the site is hosted. Here's the actual process and when not to do it.
article_domain_transfer.lead: "I want to switch registrars but I'm worried the site will go down mid-transfer" is a common concern, and the reason many people tolerate poor service or steep renewal pricing. In practice a domain transfer does **not** touch your DNS — as long as you don't change nameservers yourself, your site and mail keep running throughout. What actually needs attention isn't downtime; it's timing and lock rules.

seo.title: Domain Transfer Guide | Auth Codes, Timing & Zero Downtime
seo.description: A domain transfer won't take your site offline. What changes and what doesn't, how to get the EPP auth code, the five-day auto-approval rule, and when not to transfer.

s1.title: What a Transfer Actually Changes
s1.p1: The fastest way to kill the downtime worry is to be clear about what a transfer actually touches. A domain's registration and its DNS resolution are separate things: the registrar handles the first (who owns this domain, who you pay), and the nameservers handle the second (which machine this domain points at).
s1.p2: A transfer only swaps the first one. Your nameserver settings carry over untouched, so site, mail, and certificate validation all keep working. The table below sets out exactly what changes and what doesn't.
s1.p3: The one situation that does cause downtime is **changing nameservers at the same time as transferring**. Do those two things separately, a few days apart, and there is no interruption risk at all.

table.caption: What a domain transfer changes and doesn't. Nearly all downtime fear comes from misreading the second row.
table.r1c3: Billing, control panel, and support move to the new registrar
table.r2c3: Unless you change them yourself, site and mail run throughout
table.r3c3: Added to the existing expiry, not restarted from the transfer date
table.r4c3: Ownership isn't affected; the WHOIS registrant stays as it was

s2.title: Three Things to Sort Out First
s2.intro: A transfer stalls without any one of these, so confirm all three before starting:
s2.r1_desc: Turn off Registrar Lock (`clientTransferProhibited`) in your current registrar's control panel. This lock should normally stay on to prevent hijacking — you only lift it to transfer. Once removed, the WHOIS status shows `ok` or `clientTransferPeriod`.
s2.r2_desc: The EPP code (also called an auth code or transfer key) is a string generated by your current registrar proving you're authorised to move the domain. Most registrars display it in the panel or email it to the admin address. Under ICANN rules the registrar must release it to you **within five calendar days** and may not stall without cause.
s2.r3_title: 3. Confirm you can receive mail at the admin address
s2.r3_desc: The confirmation email goes to the admin contact in WHOIS. If that mailbox is long abandoned — or worse, hosted on the very domain you're moving — you won't receive it and the transfer deadlocks. Update it to an address you actually use and that doesn't depend on this domain. Note that changing registrant details can trigger a 60-day lock, so do this **well in advance**.

s3.title: The Process and the Timing
s3.p1: With the prerequisites in place the process is simple: order the transfer at the **new** registrar, enter the auth code, pay (a transfer usually costs the same as a one-year renewal), and wait for confirmation. The new registrar sends a confirmation email for you to approve, and your current registrar notifies you as well.
s3.p2: Then you wait. The losing registrar may release the domain immediately, completing the transfer in minutes. If it takes no action, ICANN rules mean the transfer **auto-approves after five days**. That waiting period is deliberate: it gives the genuine holder time to spot and stop an unauthorised transfer.
s3.callout: The practical implication: if your current registrar has no "approve" button, or you can't find it, just wait the five days — the transfer completes regardless, and chasing support won't speed it up. Conversely, if you receive a transfer notice you didn't initiate, those five days are your window to stop it, so log in to the current registrar and reject it immediately.
s3.p3: Once complete, the new expiry is the old one plus a year. Note that some TLDs — country-code domains in particular — follow different rules, with their own timing and fees, so it's worth checking that TLD's policy before you start.

s4.title: When Not to Transfer
s4.p1: Three situations make a transfer fail or cost more. First, **being inside a 60-day lock**: within 60 days of initial registration, of a previous transfer, or of changing registrant details, the domain can't move. Second, **being too close to expiry**: a transfer takes days, and starting one a few days before expiry risks the domain lapsing mid-process, dropping you into renewal or even redemption.
s4.p2: Third, the domain **already being in the grace or redemption period**. Once the current registrar has begun deletion, it must restore the domain first (possibly for a redemption fee) before any transfer. So if you're planning to switch and expiry is close, the correct order is **renew at the current registrar first, then transfer at your leisure** — the transfer adds a year anyway, so nothing is wasted.

s5.title: Three Habits That Keep You Online
s5.intro: The transfer itself doesn't touch DNS, but these are worth doing anyway:
s5.l1_title: 1. Back up your DNS records first
s5.l1_desc: If you use your current registrar's own DNS service rather than an external provider, those records may not follow the domain across. Screenshot or export every A, CNAME, MX, and TXT record first so you can rebuild quickly if needed. On external DNS this doesn't apply at all.
s5.l2_title: 2. Don't change nameservers at the same time
s5.l2_desc: Transferring and changing DNS are independent operations — do them separately. Complete the transfer, confirm everything works for a few days, then change DNS if you still need to. Done together, any problem leaves you unable to tell which caused it.
s5.l3_title: 3. Keep access to the old registrar account
s5.l3_desc: Don't rush to close the old account once the transfer completes. Leave it for a few weeks in case you need to check historical settings or billing records. Deal with it after the new registrar has proven stable.

s6.title: Pre-Transfer Checklist
s6.c1_title: You're not inside any lock period
s6.c1_desc: Check the registration date, the date of any previous transfer, and whether registrant details changed recently. Any of those within 60 days blocks the move.
s6.c2_desc: Leave at least 15 days of buffer. If expiry is close, renew first rather than risk lapsing mid-transfer.
s6.c3_title: The admin mailbox actually receives mail
s6.c3_desc: Send yourself a test message. Check especially whether that mailbox is hosted on the domain you're about to move — that's the classic deadlock.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: A domain transfer is simpler than most people expect: unlock, get the auth code, order at the new registrar, wait up to five days. The site doesn't go down, because DNS was never part of the transfer. What genuinely needs care is the two timing issues — lock periods and expiry dates — and avoiding those makes the process near-foolproof.
s7.p2: If you're moving because renewals got expensive, remember to check the new registrar's **standard renewal price** rather than the first-year promotion. Our domain registration guide covers that in detail, and it applies equally after a transfer.

s1.title: A Domain Is Rented, Not Bought
s1.p1: Registering a domain gets you exclusive use for a defined term, typically one to ten years — not permanent ownership. Keep renewing and you can hold it indefinitely; miss once and it enters a reclamation process on a fixed schedule, where every stage costs more to reverse than the last.
s1.p2: Most people have no idea what that process looks like until a site goes dark one morning. The four standard stages are below. Pay particular attention to the third — that's where the expensive surprise lives.
s1.p3: Worth stressing: by the time a domain reaches the grace period, DNS resolution has usually already stopped. So if you discover the problem because the site broke, the clock has been running for a while. That's exactly why auto-renew and expiry monitoring have to be set up in advance rather than sorted out during an incident.

table.caption: What happens after a domain expires. Exact durations vary by registrar and TLD, but the stage structure is consistent.
table.r1c3: Normal use; can renew and transfer registrar
table.r2c3: DNS has usually stopped, but you can still renew at the normal price
table.r3c3: Requires a redemption fee, commonly USD 80–100 or more
table.r4c3: No longer recoverable; then open for anyone to register

s2.title: Three Things That Matter When Picking a TLD
s2.intro: The TLD is the last part of the domain (.com, .tw, .io…). These are what actually deserve weight:
s2.r1_desc: `.com` remains the most universally recognised and the one you never have to explain. If your customers are in Taiwan and local identity helps, `.tw` or `.com.tw` earns something. Conversely, obscure new gTLDs may be memorable but still carry lower trust with some users and corporate procurement processes — worth weighing in B2B contexts.
s2.r2_title: The renewal price, not the first-year price
s2.r2_desc: Many new gTLDs attract registrations with a very low first year while the renewal is several times that, with no cap guaranteed. Look up the TLD's **standard renewal price** and multiply by the years you expect to hold it. That's the real cost.
s2.r3_desc: Some TLDs restrict who may register (a local registered entity, a particular industry), and some have unusual dispute or transfer rules. Obscure TLDs carry one rarely-mentioned risk too: if the registry operator struggles commercially, long-term stability is weaker than with mainstream choices.

s3.title: What Actually Differs Between Registrars
s3.p1: Most of the difference between registrars isn't the first-year price — it's the terms you won't notice at signup but will meet every year afterwards. First is **renewal pricing**: promotional rates usually apply to year one only, reverting to standard price from year two, and the gap can be large.
s3.p2: Second is **whether WHOIS privacy is free**. Registration details are public by default — name, address, phone, email — and privacy protection substitutes proxy details for those fields. Some registrars include it free for the life of the domain; others bill annually, which adds up considerably over time.
s3.callout: Working out the ten-year total is the single best way to avoid this trap: first-year promotional price + standard renewal × 9 years + privacy protection (if billed separately). Compare on that number and the cheapest first year frequently turns out to be the most expensive overall.
s3.p3: Third are the **attached conditions**: whether transferring out costs anything, whether you're forced onto the registrar's own DNS, and whether a DNS management API exists. That last one matters especially to teams automating things — if you intend to issue SSL certificates automatically via ACME with DNS validation, whether your registrar exposes an API decides whether that's possible at all.

s4.title: Transfer Locks: The Real Rules, and What's Changing
s4.p1: Moving a domain to another registrar runs into ICANN's transfer lock rules. Three situations currently trigger a 60-day hold: **within 60 days of initial registration**, **within 60 days of a previous transfer**, and **within 60 days of changing registrant contact details** (most registrars let you opt out of that last one in advance). Separately, the transfer authorisation code (EPP code) must be released to you within five calendar days.
s4.p2: Here's the part most articles get wrong: this rule **is changing, but hasn't landed**. ICANN's GNSO Council approved reform recommendations in late 2024 that would shorten the 60-day hold to 30 days (720 hours), but it still requires Board approval and registrar implementation, and no timeline is settled. So both "it's been abolished" and "it's a fixed 60 days" are currently imprecise — most registrars are still enforcing 60 days in practice, so confirm the current rule with yours before planning a transfer.

s5.title: Three Protective Settings Worth Doing Now
s5.intro: These three take under ten minutes and prevent most of the disasters:
s5.l1_desc: This flags the domain `clientTransferProhibited`, blocking unauthorised transfers out. It's the most basic and most effective defence against domain hijacking. It's usually on by default, but it's worth confirming yourself, and you simply lift it when you genuinely want to transfer.
s5.l2_title: 2. Auto-renew — and verify the payment method
s5.l2_desc: Auto-renew alone isn't enough. The most common failure is an expired card nobody noticed: the renewal charge fails, and the domain lapses anyway. Put the card's expiry in your calendar too, and make sure renewal notices go to a mailbox somebody actually reads.
s5.l3_title: 3. WHOIS privacy and a separate admin mailbox
s5.l3_desc: Enable privacy so your contact details aren't publicly harvested. And critically, **don't use an address on this domain** as the registrar account contact — if the domain breaks and mail stops, you won't receive the password reset needed to fix it. Use a separate domain or a free mail service for that contact.

s6.title: Three Things to Confirm Before Registering
s6.intro: Before you pay, establish these three:
s6.c1_desc: Not the first-year promotion. Find the TLD's standard renewal figure and multiply by the years you expect to hold it.
s6.c2_title: Transfer-out policy and how to get the auth code
s6.c2_desc: Whether transferring out costs anything, where the auth code lives in the control panel, and whether support has to be involved. This determines whether you can leave later.
s6.c3_desc: Whether you can set arbitrary DNS records yourself, and whether an API exists. If you plan certificate automation or CDN integration, this is a hard requirement.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: Domains are cheap, but a domain is the root of the whole online presence — site, mail, and certificate validation all hang off it. The real cost and risk aren't in the registration fee; they're in renewal pricing, transfer flexibility, and whether you configured auto-renew and locking. Ten minutes on those three settings beats a redemption fee later by a wide margin.
s7.p2: If your domain already fronts a CDN or you issue certificates frequently, DNS API support directly determines whether that can be automated. Our SSL automation platform integrates with major DNS providers for exactly that — automatic validation and multi-node deployment.

article_china_latency.short_title: Why Connections to China Are Slow
article_china_latency.title: Why Are Connections to China So Slow? It Isn't Just the Firewall
article_china_latency.excerpt: Most people blame the Great Firewall first. In practice, latency and packet loss usually come from three structural factors unrelated to censorship: inter-carrier bottlenecks, concentrated international gateways, and return-path route quality.
article_china_latency.lead: "Our site won't load in China." "Customers there say it's slow." Almost every team doing cross-border business hits this, and the firewall is usually the first suspect. It exists and it does have effects — but attributing everything to it tends to make you miss the parts you can actually fix. In practice, most latency and packet loss comes down to three purely structural network problems.

seo.title: Why Connections to China Are Slow | Routes & Gateways
seo.description: A technical breakdown of why network access to China is slow: inter-carrier interconnection bottlenecks, international gateways concentrated in Beijing/Shanghai/Guangzhou, the difference between 163 and CN2 GIA return routes, and what can be improved.
seo.keywords: China network latency, slow connection to China, CN2 GIA, 163 backbone, return route, China interconnection, cross-border network optimization, China CDN

s1.title: Break "Slow" Apart First
s1.p1: "Slow" isn't one problem — it's a label covering several distinct ones. High latency, packet loss, slow only in the evening, specific services unreachable: these four symptoms have entirely different causes and entirely different fixes. Discussing them as one thing produces the unactionable conclusion that "Chinese networks are just like that."
s1.p2: Before optimising anything, establish which one you actually have. The table below maps four common symptoms to their causes and how to identify them. Most teams discover they have more than one at once.
s1.p3: Worth stating up front: of these four, only the last is directly related to content filtering. The first three are purely questions of network capacity and routing — and they're what the rest of this article unpacks, because they're also the ones you have a realistic chance of improving.

table.caption: Four common symptoms, their causes, and how to identify them. Most teams have more than one.
table.r1c3: Run traceroute; check hop count and path
table.r2c1: Fine by day, slow at night
table.r2c3: Test at off-peak and evening peak, then compare
table.r3c1: Latency OK but noticeable packet loss
table.r3c3: Test outbound and return paths separately
table.r4c1: A specific domain won't load at all
table.r4c3: Test the same host via a different domain or IP

s2.title: The Three Real Structural Causes
s2.intro: None of the following relates to content filtering. They're consequences of network capacity and commercial settlement — and they account for most cross-border connection problems:
s2.r1_desc: China Telecom, Unicom, and Mobile each run independent networks and must exchange traffic at national or provincial interconnection points. Those points have finite bandwidth, and when traffic surges — evening peak, a popular video platform ramping up — they saturate and cross-network access slows immediately. This is why the same server can feel fine to a Telecom user and slow to a Unicom one. The problem isn't your server; it's the segment in between.
s2.r2_desc: On China Telecom's ChinaNet backbone, the country's international traffic ultimately funnels through three gateways: Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou. Whether a user sits in Chengdu or Shenyang, outbound international traffic detours through one of those three. That structural concentration makes the international egress a natural peak-hour bottleneck — and not one you can solve by buying more bandwidth on your own side.
s2.r3_desc: Traffic from China to overseas (the outbound leg) and from overseas back into China (the return leg) may take entirely different paths, and return quality is usually what determines what users actually feel. Different route tiers behave very differently at peak, which the next section covers in detail.

s3.title: Route Tiers: 163, CN2 GT, and CN2 GIA
s3.p1: Any discussion of cross-border quality into China runs into China Telecom's route tiers. The traditional one is the 163 backbone, whose route nodes typically begin with 202.97. It carries the overwhelming majority of international traffic, which is exactly why it congests hardest at evening peak — showing up as latency spikes and pronounced packet loss.
s3.p2: CN2 (ChinaNet Next Carrying Network) is China Telecom's later-generation carrying network, with nodes beginning 59.43. It comes in two forms. CN2 GT routes the international leg over CN2 but returns to 163 for the domestic leg, so the international link improves while the domestic segment can still congest. CN2 GIA keeps both outbound and return legs entirely on CN2 without dropping back to 163, with the fewest hops, the highest QoS priority, and deliberately lighter loading.
s3.callout: Here's an easy way to misdiagnose this: outbound and return paths are frequently asymmetric. Latency you measure from Taiwan or overseas is the outbound leg — but what users in China experience depends on the return leg. Drawing conclusions from a one-directional test often produces a verdict opposite to what users report, which is why testing both directions separately matters.
s3.p3: Practically, this means that when comparing facilities or CDN providers, "is there a CN2 GIA return path?" often determines the real experience for users in China more than raw bandwidth does. It's also the kind of thing that doesn't appear on a spec sheet, so it's worth asking about directly.

s4.title: So How Much Is the Firewall?
s4.p1: Content filtering exists and does cause connection problems, but it operates differently from the three factors above: it tends to make specific targets unreachable or unstable rather than making everything uniformly slower. If your own service isn't within scope of any restriction, the slowness users report is still most likely one of the three structural causes.
s4.p2: Put another way: if your site "loads but is slow" in China, that's usually a capacity and routing problem and architecture changes can improve it. If it "won't load at all, on any network," that's when it's worth investigating access restrictions. Separating those two cases first is what stops you spending effort in the wrong place.

s5.title: Three Practical Directions for Improvement
s5.intro: Against the structural problems above, there are three layers you can work on:
s5.l1_desc: The most direct approach is caching static content at edge nodes nearer to users in China, reducing how much traffic has to cross the international gateways at all. Nodes in Hong Kong and around China help somewhat; genuinely landing content on nodes inside the mainland requires completing ICP filing — a regulatory process that takes time and paperwork, so it's worth assessing early.
s5.l2_desc: When selecting a facility or CDN provider, ask specifically which return route is used rather than comparing bandwidth figures alone. At the same monthly cost, the difference between a CN2 GIA return path and an ordinary 163 one at evening peak is often more noticeable than doubling your bandwidth.
s5.l3_title: 3. Reduce the number of round trips
s5.l3_desc: Once per-round-trip latency can't be reduced further, reduce how many round trips you need. Enabling HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to multiplex connections, consolidating and trimming resource requests, and preloading critical assets — these front-end optimisations have amplified benefit in high-latency conditions, far more than they do on a low-latency network.

s6.title: Three Things to Do When Diagnosing
s6.intro: Before raising the issue with a provider or evaluating a fix, gather these three things — your judgement will be considerably more accurate:
s6.c1_title: Test across time windows, not once
s6.c1_desc: Cover at least off-peak and evening peak. A large gap between them points strongly at interconnect or gateway congestion rather than your server's performance.
s6.c2_desc: Telecom, Unicom, and Mobile results often differ substantially. Concluding from one carrier alone easily misreads a single-network issue as universal, or misses one entirely.
s6.c3_desc: Test from your side toward China and from China toward your server. As noted above, the paths are frequently asymmetric, and one-directional testing yields misleading conclusions.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: Slow access from China is rarely down to a single cause, and the firewall usually isn't the dominant one. Capacity limits at inter-carrier interconnection points, international egress concentrated in Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, and differences in return-route tier together explain most of the latency and packet loss seen in practice — and all three can be improved through architectural choices. That's the value of separating the causes properly.
s7.p2: If you want to see how your service currently performs across China's three carriers, our speed test platform gives you per-carrier measured data, so you can decide which direction to tackle first.

article_ssl_validity.short_title: SSL Certificate Lifetimes Drop to 200 Days
article_ssl_validity.title: SSL Certificate Lifetimes Are Now 200 Days — and 47 by 2029. What Should Your Team Do?
article_ssl_validity.excerpt: As of March 15, 2026, the maximum lifetime for a publicly trusted TLS certificate dropped from 398 days to 200, with two further reductions scheduled for 2027 and 2029. Here's the timeline, the reasoning behind it, and why manual renewal won't survive the next phase.
article_ssl_validity.lead: As of March 15, 2026, the maximum lifetime for a publicly trusted TLS/SSL certificate has dropped from 398 days to 200. This isn't one certificate authority adjusting its policy — it's an industry-wide requirement ratified by the CA/Browser Forum, with two more reductions already scheduled. For teams still managing certificates by hand, the operational burden is set to multiply over the next three years.

seo.title: SSL Lifetimes Cut to 200 Days | 2026 Schedule & Guide
seo.description: The CA/Browser Forum has scheduled phased reductions to TLS certificate lifetimes: 200 days in 2026, 100 days in 2027, and 47 days in 2029. Full timeline, real-world impact, and how to automate your response.
seo.keywords: SSL certificate lifetime, certificate validity reduction, 200 day certificates, 47 day certificates, SC-081, ACME protocol, automatic certificate renewal, SSL certificate management

s1.title: What Changed
s1.p1: The CA/Browser Forum is the industry body of certificate authorities and browser vendors that sets the shared rules for publicly trusted certificates. In April 2025 it ratified Ballot SC-081v3, which established a phased schedule for shortening TLS certificate lifetimes.
s1.p2: What makes this significant is that it isn't a commercial decision by any single certificate authority — it's a requirement every publicly trusted CA must follow. In other words, the timeline applies regardless of who you currently buy certificates from, including free services such as Let's Encrypt.
s1.p3: Worth noting: alongside certificate lifetimes, the reuse period for domain control validation (DCV) is shrinking too. That means it isn't only certificates that need reissuing more often — domain ownership itself must be revalidated more frequently, dropping to 10 days by 2029.

table.caption: The phased reduction schedule set by Ballot SC-081v3. We are currently in the 200-day phase.
table.r1c3: Old rule — roughly one renewal a year
table.r2c3: Current rule — about twice a year

s2.title: Why Shorten Certificate Lifetimes?
s2.intro: Shorter lifetimes clearly mean more work for operations teams, but there are several concrete security arguments behind the change:
s2.r1_title: Shrinking the window for key compromise
s2.r1_desc: When a private key leaks or a certificate is misused, how long an attacker can exploit it depends directly on the certificate's remaining lifetime. Going from 398 days to 47 compresses the worst-case exposure window to roughly one-eighth of what it was.
s2.r2_desc: In theory a compromised certificate can be revoked via CRL or OCSP, but in practice these mechanisms are not fully reliable — some browsers soft-fail when the check doesn't complete, and network conditions can cause timeouts. Short-lived certificates simply expire, with no dependency on revocation working correctly.
s2.r3_desc: Frequent renewal pushes the whole industry toward automated workflows. This isn't only about the current rules — it's preparation for the eventual migration to post-quantum cryptography, when the industry will need to be able to rotate certificates and algorithms quickly.

s3.title: What This Actually Costs You
s3.p1: The impact on operational workload multiplies at each phase. Under the old rules a certificate was renewed roughly once a year. In the 200-day phase that becomes about twice a year; the 100-day phase in 2027 makes it four times; and the 47-day phase in 2029 pushes it to roughly eight times a year.
s3.p2: Then multiply that by how many domains you manage. For an organization handling 20 domains and subdomains, the old rules meant about 20 certificate operations a year. In the 47-day phase, that becomes roughly 160 a year — which, done manually, is a certificate task every couple of days.
s3.callout: In practice, certificate authorities typically issue slightly under the cap (for example 199 days against the 200-day limit) to leave a safety margin. It's also worth not waiting until the final day: starting the renewal when roughly a third of the lifetime remains leaves enough room to handle a failed validation or other surprises.
s3.p3: The bigger risk is human error. Certificate management is a classic low-frequency, high-consequence task: it needs no attention at all, right up until a renewal is missed — at which point the site throws browser security warnings, API calls start failing, and payment integrations can break. Multiplying the frequency by eight multiplies the opportunities to get it wrong.

s4.title: Why Manual Processes Won't Hold
s4.p1: A full manual renewal usually involves: logging into the CA portal to submit the request, adding a TXT or CNAME record in DNS for validation, waiting for validation to pass, downloading the certificate files, uploading them to every server or CDN node one at a time, reloading the service configuration, and finally confirming the new certificate is actually being served. When everything goes smoothly, that's roughly 20 to 40 minutes.
s4.p2: Multiply that by domain count and renewal frequency and the cost adds up quickly. Worse, this work resists any fixed rhythm — every certificate has its own expiry date scattered across the year, so someone has to keep tracking them. Once a team manages a few dozen domains, simply knowing which certificate expires when becomes a list that needs maintaining in its own right.

s5.title: How to Respond: Three Layers of Automation
s5.intro: The direction is clear — take the human out of the loop. But automation isn't a single step; it's three layers you can adopt progressively:
s5.l1_title: Layer one: automated issuance and renewal
s5.l1_desc: The ACME protocol (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) lets a server talk directly to a certificate authority to request, validate, and renew automatically. Let's Encrypt with Certbot is the most common pairing, and most hosting control panels now ship something equivalent. This layer solves where the certificate comes from.
s5.l2_desc: Among ACME's validation methods, HTTP validation requires exposing a specific path publicly, which isn't always convenient; DNS validation requires adding TXT records dynamically. Creating those records automatically through your DNS provider's API removes the manual login step entirely and makes wildcard certificate automation possible. Given that the DCV reuse period is shrinking too, this layer only grows in importance.
s5.l3_desc: Obtaining the certificate is only half the job. The genuinely time-consuming part is deployment — pushing the same certificate to multiple servers, multiple CDN nodes, sometimes across different CDN vendors. Without automation here, the time saved in the first two layers gets eaten at the deployment stage. Ideally, a newly issued certificate propagates to every node that needs it and its status is verified automatically.

s6.title: Three Things to Do Now
s6.intro: If your team hasn't audited its exposure to this change yet, start with these three steps:
s6.c1_desc: List every certificate in use, including the domain, issuing CA, expiry date, where it's deployed (which servers, which CDNs), and who currently owns renewal. Building this list alone tends to surface a few forgotten certificates.
s6.c2_title: Separate what can be automated from what can't
s6.c2_desc: Most modern environments can adopt ACME, but some legacy systems, air-gapped networks, or specialized hardware may not support it directly. Flagging these exceptions early is what lets you estimate the extra handling cost — or decide whether the architecture itself should change.
s6.c3_title: Set up expiry monitoring and alerts
s6.c3_desc: Even with automation in place, you still need independent monitoring to confirm renewals actually succeeded. Alerting ahead of expiry is the last line of defense against an automated pipeline failing silently.

s7.title: In Summary
s7.p1: The direction of travel is settled and the dates are known. The 200-day phase might still be survivable with manual effort, but the 100-day phase in 2027 and the 47-day phase in 2029 effectively rule manual management out. Rather than waiting until the workload has already doubled, it's worth using the remaining runway to get automation in place.
s7.p2: If you're evaluating certificate automation, or want to understand how to automate deployment as well as issuance, our technical team is happy to talk through your specific setup.

article_vps_guide.title: How to Choose a VPS: Reading the Specs, Setting the Budget, and Avoiding the Traps
article_vps_guide.excerpt: What actually separates shared hosting, VPS, and dedicated servers? How much CPU and memory do you need? And why does the bill triple at renewal? A repeatable process for choosing a VPS.
article_vps_guide.lead: "How many cores and how much RAM should I get?" is the most common question when choosing a VPS, and the hardest to answer directly — because it depends on what you run, what your traffic looks like, and how much of your own time you want to spend on operations. This guide avoids brand comparisons and instead separates the decision into three dimensions: specs, budget, and contract terms.

seo.title: How to Choose a VPS | Specs, Budget & Renewal Traps - Kineticlinks
seo.description: A practical VPS buying guide: how shared hosting differs from VPS, how to size CPU and memory, why data center location matters, and the renewal pricing traps to watch for.

s1.title: First: Do You Actually Need a VPS?
s1.p1: Hosting comes in roughly four shapes, distinguished by whether resources are exclusively yours and how much operations work falls to you. Plenty of people jump straight to a VPS and discover they needed neither the resources nor the administration burden. Others stay on shared hosting until traffic finally breaks the site.
s1.p2: The rule of thumb is simple. If you don't need to install unusual packages, don't need to change server configuration, and your traffic is steady and modest, shared hosting is enough. The moment you need full system access — a specific PHP version, background jobs, your own database — or shared performance becomes unpredictable, that's when a VPS earns its cost.
s1.p3: Conversely, if your compute needs have grown to consume a whole physical machine, or regulation requires data to sit in a specific physical environment, the answer is a dedicated server or colocation — not endlessly scaling a VPS upward.

table.caption: How the four hosting types differ. Most small and mid-sized sites sit between shared hosting and VPS.
